**Activity 1: Your First Swing Window (JFrame)** 

**Purpose** 

Create a working Swing application with a main window. This is the foundation of every Swing  application you will ever build. 

**Learning Outcome addressed:** \#1, \#3 

**Time:** 45 minutes 

 **Real-World Application** 

Every desktop application you've ever used started with a main window just like the one you're  about to build: 

• **Microsoft Word** — starts with a JFrame (or its equivalent in Windows) • **Notepad++** — a Swing app with a main window 

• **The NetBeans IDE** — built entirely on Swing 

• **POS terminals** — the cashier's screen is a Swing JFrame 

When you create your first JFrame, you are creating the container that will hold **every button,  text field, menu, and panel** in your application.

**Step 1.2: Create Your First JFrame** 

Go to activity1-first-window/. Create FirstWindow.java:

*// \============================================================ // FIRST SWING WINDOW* 

*// \============================================================ // This is the simplest possible Swing application.* 

*// It creates a JFrame (main window) and displays it.*

Page **5** of **82**   
*// \============================================================* import javax.swing.\*; *// Swing components (JFrame, JButton, etc.)* public class FirstWindow { 

 public static void main(String\[\] args) { 

 *// CRITICAL: All Swing code must run on the EDT.* 

 *// This is the golden rule of Swing programming.* 

 SwingUtilities.invokeLater(() \-\> { 

 createAndShowWindow(); 

 }); 

 } 

 private static void createAndShowWindow() { 

 *// 1\. Create the JFrame (the main window)* 

 JFrame frame \= new JFrame("My First Swing App"); 

 *// 2\. Set what happens when the user clicks the X button  // EXIT\_ON\_CLOSE terminates the JVM when the window closes*  frame.setDefaultCloseOperation(JFrame.EXIT\_ON\_CLOSE); 

 *// 3\. Set the window's size in pixels (width x height)* 

 frame.setSize(500, 400);

Page **6** of **82**   
 *// 4\. Center the window on the screen* 

 frame.setLocationRelativeTo(null); 

 *// 5\. Make the window visible (hidden by default)* 

 frame.setVisible(true); 

 *// Log to console to prove we're on the EDT* 

 System.out.println("Window created on thread: " 

 \+ Thread.currentThread().getName()); 

 } 

} 

**Save the file** (Ctrl \+ S).

**Step 1.5: Self-Check Questions** 

**Q1: What is the difference between** JFrame **and the content pane?** 

\`JFrame\` is the top-level window (with title bar, minimize/maximize/close buttons). The content  pane is the invisible container inside the JFrame where you add components. In modern Swing,  \`frame.add(component)\` automatically adds to the content pane.  

**Q2: What does** EXIT\_ON\_CLOSE **do?** 

It sets the behavior when the user clicks the X button — the JVM terminates completely. Other  options include \`DO\_NOTHING\_ON\_CLOSE\`, \`HIDE\_ON\_CLOSE\`, and \`DISPOSE\_ON\_CLOSE\`.  

**Q3: Why did we wrap the code in** SwingUtilities.invokeLater()**?** 

Because all Swing GUI creation and manipulation must happen on the EDT. Calling  \`invokeLater()\` schedules the code to run on the EDT, ensuring thread safety.

**Step 2.4: Self-Check Questions** 

**Q1: What is the difference between** JTextField **and** JTextArea**?** 

\`JTextField\` is a single-line input; \`JTextArea\` is multi-line. Use \`JTextField\` for short inputs (name,  email) and \`JTextArea\` for longer text (comments, descriptions).  

**Q2: Why do we put** JRadioButton**s inside a** ButtonGroup**?** 

To enforce that only one radio button can be selected at a time. Without a \`ButtonGroup\`,  multiple radio buttons can be selected simultaneously.  

**Q3: Why does the** JTextArea **need a** JScrollPane**?** 

Because \`JTextArea\` doesn't have built-in scrollbars. Wrapping it in a \`JScrollPane\` adds  scrollbars automatically when text exceeds the visible area.

**Step 3.5: Layout Choice Guide** 

| Scenario  | Best Layout |
| :---- | :---- |
| Row of buttons at the top  | FlowLayout (LEFT aligned) |
| Main window with header, footer,  sidebar | BorderLayout |
| Grid of images or buttons  | GridLayout |
| Vertical stack of items  | BoxLayout (Y\_AXIS) or GridLayout(0, 1\) |
| Complex form with labels and fields  | GridBagLayout or nested panels |
| Centered element | FlowLayout (CENTER) inside a BorderLayout  CENTER |
| Toolbar  | FlowLayout |
| Login form  | GridLayout(3, 2\) or nested FlowLayouts |

**Step 3.6: Self-Check Questions** 

**Q1: When would you choose** GridLayout **over** FlowLayout**?**

Page **23** of **82**   
Use \`GridLayout\` when you need equal-sized cells in a fixed grid (like a calculator or photo  gallery). Use \`FlowLayout\` when you want components to flow naturally and wrap at the edge of  the container.  

**Q2: Why do we often nest layout managers?** 

no single layout manager handles every situation. By nesting panels (each with its own layout),  you can build complex UIs. This is how real applications are built.  

**Q3: What does** BorderLayout.CENTER **do differently from the other regions?** 

CENTER expands to fill all remaining space. The other four regions only take up as much space  as they need.  

**Troubleshooting Activity 3** 

| Problem  | Fix |
| :---- | ----- |
| Buttons are tiny or invisible  | GridLayout needs a container size; try frame.pack() or setSize() |
| Layout doesn't update after  resizing | Normal — layout managers recalculate automatically |
| Component added twice | Check the region — BorderLayout only shows the last  component per region |
| Buttons overlap | You're probably using absolute positioning (setBounds) — use  a layout manager instead |

**Activity 4: The EDT Rule — Why and How** 

**Purpose**

Page **24** of **82**   
Master the Event Dispatch Thread rule. Understand why it exists, and how to comply with it. **Learning Outcome addressed:** \#3 

**Time:** 60 minutes 

 **Real-World Application** 

**Ever seen a frozen app?** 

• A **Windows Explorer** window that stops responding while copying files • A **browser tab** that freezes while loading a huge page 

• An **IDE** that locks up while compiling a large project 

All of these are EDT violations. The developer accidentally ran a long operation on the UI thread,  and the app "froze." 

**What proper EDT usage gives you:** A **responsive** app that never freezes — like Word, Excel, or  VS Code. Users can still click buttons and type while background operations run. 

**Step 4.1: Demonstrate the Problem — Freezing the UI** 

Go to activity4-edt-rule/. Create FreezeDemo.java: 

java 

import javax.swing.\*; 

import java.awt.\*; 

public class FreezeDemo { 

 public static void main(String\[\] args) { 

 SwingUtilities.invokeLater(() \-\> { 

 JFrame frame \= new JFrame("EDT Demo — BAD Practice"); 

 frame.setDefaultCloseOperation(JFrame.EXIT\_ON\_CLOSE); 

 frame.setSize(400, 200); 

 frame.setLocationRelativeTo(null); 

 frame.setLayout(new FlowLayout());

Page **25** of **82**   
 JLabel status \= new JLabel("Ready"); 

 JButton button \= new JButton("Freeze the UI"); 

 *// BAD: This blocks the EDT for 5 seconds\!*  button.addActionListener(e \-\> { 

 status.setText("Working..."); 

 try { 

 Thread.sleep(5000); *// Simulates a long operation*  } catch (InterruptedException ex) { } 

 status.setText("Done\!"); 

 }); 

 frame.add(button); 

 frame.add(status); 

 frame.setVisible(true); 

 }); 

 } 

} 

**Run it. Then:** 

1\. Click the "Freeze the UI" button. 

2\. **Try to move the window** — you can't\! 

3\. **Try to resize the window** — no response\! 

4\. **Try clicking the button again** — nothing happens\! 5\. **Wait 5 seconds** — the button finally updates to "Done\!"

Page **26** of **82**   
**What happened?** The Thread.sleep(5000) on the EDT blocked the event loop, so **nothing else  could happen** for 5 seconds. 

**Step 4.2: Fix It — Using a Background Thread** 

Now create FixedDemo.java: 

java 

import javax.swing.\*; 

import java.awt.\*; 

public class FixedDemo { 

 public static void main(String\[\] args) { 

 SwingUtilities.invokeLater(() \-\> { 

 JFrame frame \= new JFrame("EDT Demo — GOOD Practice"); 

 frame.setDefaultCloseOperation(JFrame.EXIT\_ON\_CLOSE); 

 frame.setSize(400, 200); 

 frame.setLocationRelativeTo(null); 

 frame.setLayout(new FlowLayout()); 

 JLabel status \= new JLabel("Ready"); 

 JButton button \= new JButton("Do Long Operation"); 

 *// GOOD: Run the long operation in a background thread* 

 button.addActionListener(e \-\> { 

 status.setText("Working..."); 

 button.setEnabled(false);

Page **27** of **82**   
 *// Start a background thread* 

 new Thread(() \-\> { 

 try { 

 Thread.sleep(5000); *// Blocks THIS thread, not the EDT*  } catch (InterruptedException ex) { } 

 *// CRITICAL: Update GUI on the EDT* 

 SwingUtilities.invokeLater(() \-\> { 

 status.setText("Done\!"); 

 button.setEnabled(true); 

 }); 

 }).start(); 

 }); 

 frame.add(button); 

 frame.add(status); 

 frame.setVisible(true); 

 }); 

 } 

} 

**Run it. Then:** 

1\. Click "Do Long Operation". 

2\. The status shows "Working..." and the button grays out. 3\. **Now try to move the window** — it moves freely\! 4\. **Try to resize it** — it resizes\! 

5\. **Notice the difference** — the UI stays responsive\!

**Step 4.3: The Two Golden Rules** 

**Rule 1: All GUI creation and updates must happen on the EDT.** java 

*// Correct* 

SwingUtilities.invokeLater(() \-\> { 

 label.setText("Updated\!"); 

}); 

*// Wrong (from a background thread)* 

label.setText("Updated\!"); *// Thread violation\!* 

**Rule 2: Never perform long operations on the EDT.** java 

*// Correct — run in background, update on EDT* new Thread(() \-\> { 

 String result \= downloadFile(); *// background work*  SwingUtilities.invokeLater(() \-\> { 

 statusLabel.setText(result); *// GUI update on EDT*  }); 

}).start(); 

*// Wrong — blocks the EDT* 

String result \= downloadFile(); *// EDT freezes\!* 

**Step 4.4: Check Which Thread You're On** 

Add this line to any method to verify:

Page **29** of **82**   
java 

System.out.println("Currently on: " \+ Thread.currentThread().getName()); 

| Thread Name  | Meaning |
| :---- | ----- |
| AWT-EventQueue-0  | You're on the EDT  |
| Main  | You're on the main thread (bad for GUI) |
| Thread-0, Thread-1  | You're on a background thread |

 

**Step 4.5: Self-Check Questions** 

**Q1: Why does** Thread.sleep() **on the EDT freeze the UI?** 

The EDT runs the event loop, which processes all events. If the loop is busy sleeping, it can't  process any other events, so the UI can't repaint, respond to clicks, or resize.  

**Q2: What is the safe way to update a label from a background thread?** 

Use \`SwingUtilities.invokeLater(() \-\> label.setText("..."))\`. This schedules the update to run on  the EDT.  

**Q3: What happens if you violate the EDT rule?** 

Best case: The UI freezes. Worst case: The UI glitches, displays stale data, or crashes. Swing is  not thread-safe — the rules exist to prevent subtle bugs.

| Crashes when updating  GUI | You forgot SwingUtilities.invokeLater() |
| IllegalStateException  | You're trying to update the GUI from a non-EDT thread |

**Step 5.4: Self-Check Questions** 

**Q1: How many different layout managers did you use in this mockup?** 

At least four: \`BorderLayout\` (main frame \+ header \+ status bar), \`GridLayout\` (sidebar \+ cards),  \`BoxLayout\` (main content vertical stacking), and \`FlowLayout\` implicitly inside panels. This is a  realistic combination. 

Page **39** of **82**   
**Q2: Why do we use** Box.createVerticalStrut(20) **between components?** 

To add vertical spacing. \`Box.createVerticalStrut(20)\` inserts an invisible 20-pixel-tall spacer — much cleaner than adding empty panels or margins. 

**Q3: What is the purpose of** setPreferredSize() **on the sidebar?** 

It gives the sidebar a fixed width of 180 pixels. Without it, \`BorderLayout.WEST\` would make the  sidebar shrink to the minimum needed by its contents.  

**Troubleshooting Activity 5** 

| Problem  | Fix |
| :---- | :---- |
| Sidebar is too narrow/wide  | Adjust setPreferredSize(new Dimension(180, 0)) |
| Cards look stretched  | Use setMaximumSize() on the cards panel |
| Emoji characters don't appear  | Your font may not support emoji — replace with "★"  or remove |
| Components are left-aligned but  should be centered | Use setAlignmentX(Component.CENTER\_ALIGNMENT) |

**Step 3.7: Self-Check Questions** 

**Q1: When would you choose** GridLayout **over** FlowLayout**?** 

Use \`GridLayout\` for uniformly-sized cells in a fixed grid (calculators, photo galleries). Use  \`FlowLayout\` for natural, wrapping arrangement (toolbars, tag lists).  

**Q2: Why did we nest panels inside the BorderLayout?** 

Because BorderLayout has only 5 regions. To place multiple components in one region (like 4  toolbar buttons in the North), you nest a panel with its own layout inside that region.  

**Q3: What does Matisse do automatically when you drag a component to a BorderLayout  region?** 

Matisse detects the nearest region boundary and snaps the component to NORTH, SOUTH,  EAST, WEST, or CENTER based on where you dropped it. \</details\>

**Activity 4: Understanding the EDT (Generated by NetBeans)** 

**Purpose** 

Learn how NetBeans handles the EDT rule automatically — and what happens if you break the  rule by putting long operations in event handlers. 

**Learning Outcome addressed:** \#3 

**Time:** 45 minutes 

 **Real-World Application** 

**Ever seen a frozen app?** 

• A Windows Explorer window that stops responding while copying files • A browser that freezes on a heavy page

Page **64** of **82**   
• An IDE that locks up during compile 

All of these are EDT violations. **NetBeans generates EDT-safe code for you automatically** — but  you can still break it by putting long tasks inside event handlers. This activity teaches you what  to avoid. 

**Step 4.1: Create a Project** 

1\. **File → New Project → Java Application** 

2\. **Project Name:** EDTDemo 

3\. **Location:** Browse to: 

C:\\Users\\RUICT\\Desktop\\projects\\event-driven-programming-java\\week03-swing-gui\\activity4- edt-rule 

4\. Uncheck "Create Main Class" → **Finish** 

**Step 4.2: Create the Form** 

1\. Right-click project → **New → JFrame Form** 

2\. **Class Name:** FreezeForm 

3\. Click **Finish** 

**Step 4.3: Design the UI** 

1\. Set **title** \= EDT Demo — BAD Practice 

2\. Right-click canvas → **Set Layout → Flow Layout** 

3\. Drag a **Label** → set **text** \= Ready 

4\. Drag a **Button** → set **text** \= Freeze the UI 

**Step 4.4: Wire Up the Button (The BAD Way)** 

1\. **Right-click** the button → **Events → Action → actionPerformed** 

2\. NetBeans switches to **Source** view and creates an empty method 

3\. Type this inside: 

java 

private void jButton1ActionPerformed(java.awt.event.ActionEvent evt) { 

Page **65** of **82**   
 jLabel1.setText("Working..."); 

 try { 

 Thread.sleep(5000); *// BAD: Blocks the EDT\!* 

 } catch (InterruptedException ex) { } 

 jLabel1.setText("Done\!"); 

}  

4\. Switch back to **Design** view (click the **Design** button at the top) 

**Step 4.5: Run and Observe the Problem** 

1\. Press **F6** 

2\. Click **"Freeze the UI"** 

3\. **Try to:** 

o Move the window → Can't\! 

o Resize it → Can't\! 

o Click the button again → Nothing\! 

4\. **Wait 5 seconds** → the label updates to "Done\!" 

**What happened?** The Thread.sleep(5000) inside the action listener ran on the EDT, blocking the  entire event loop. 

**Step 4.6: The GOOD Way** 

Now let's fix it. 

1\. Right-click the button → **Events → Action → actionPerformed** → NetBeans **replaces** the  method body (it was already wired, so just edit it) 

2\. Replace the method body with: 

java 

private void jButton1ActionPerformed(java.awt.event.ActionEvent evt) {   jLabel1.setText("Working...");

Page **66** of **82**   
 jButton1.setEnabled(false); 

 *// GOOD: Run the long task on a background thread* 

 new Thread(() \-\> { 

 try { 

 Thread.sleep(5000); 

 } catch (InterruptedException ex) { } 


 *// CRITICAL: Update GUI on the EDT* 

 javax.swing.SwingUtilities.invokeLater(() \-\> { 

 jLabel1.setText("Done\!"); 

 jButton1.setEnabled(true); 

 }); 

 }).start(); 

}  

**Step 4.7: Run and Observe the Fix** 

1\. Press **F6** 

2\. Click **"Freeze the UI"** 

3\. **Now try to:** 

o Move the window → Works\! 

o Resize it → Works\! 

o Click the button → It's disabled (as designed) 

The window **stays responsive** because the long task runs on a separate thread. 

**Step 4.8: See What NetBeans Did Automatically** 

1\. Switch to **Source** view

Page **67** of **82**   
2\. Scroll to the top of the file 

3\. Find the main method: 

java 

public static void main(String args\[\]) { 

 java.awt.EventQueue.invokeLater(new Runnable() { 

 public void run() { 

 new FreezeForm().setVisible(true); 

 } 

 }); 

} 

**Notice:** NetBeans automatically wrapped the GUI creation in EventQueue.invokeLater() — this is  the **EDT rule**. You didn't have to write it\! 

**Every form NetBeans creates is EDT-safe by default.** But when you write event handler code,  you must follow the two golden rules. 

**Step 4.9: The Two Golden Rules** 

**Rule 1: All GUI creation and updates must happen on the EDT.** 

java 

*// Correct* 

SwingUtilities.invokeLater(() \-\> { 

 label.setText("Updated\!"); 

}); 

**Rule 2: Never perform long operations on the EDT.** 

java 

*// Correct — run in background, update on EDT* 

new Thread(() \-\> {

Page **68** of **82**   
 String result \= longOperation(); 

 SwingUtilities.invokeLater(() \-\> label.setText(result)); 

}).start(); 

**Step 4.10: Self-Check Questions** 

**Q1: Why does NetBeans wrap GUI creation in** EventQueue.invokeLater()**?** 

Because Swing is not thread-safe. All GUI components must be created on the EDT. NetBeans  follows this rule automatically to keep your app safe.  

**Q2: What does** Thread.sleep() **do to the EDT?** 

It blocks the EDT for the specified duration. During this time, the event loop cannot process any  events — clicks, repaints, resizes. The UI freezes.  

**Q3: How do you safely update a label from a background thread?** 

Use \`SwingUtilities.invokeLater(() \-\> label.setText("..."))\` to schedule the update on the EDT.  

**Troubleshooting Activity 4** 

| Problem  | Fix |
| :---- | :---- |
| Window doesn't freeze | Make sure Thread.sleep() is inside the event handler (not in the  constructor) |
| UI still freezes after fix  | Check that Thread.sleep() is inside the new Thread(...) block |
| Crashes when updating  the label | You forgot SwingUtilities.invokeLater() |
| Can't find the "Events"  menu | Right-click on the button in **Design** view, not Source view |
